meta.title: The Explore-Before-Explain Guidebook for Science Education
meta.author: Patrick Brown

parts.title: The Explore-Before-Explain Guidebook for Science Education
parts.body: This guidebook, authored by Pat Brown, emphasizes an Explore-Before-Explain instructional sequence for science education, aiming to foster active meaning-making in students. It guides educators in designing lessons where conceptual understandings are built on evidence-based experiences, encouraging students to ponder patterns, identify cause-and-effect relationships, and develop critical thinking over just validating ideas. The book provides content and module examples relevant for K-12 science teachers and administrators, aligning with contemporary standards and safety in science. It's designed to enhance curriculum with active sensemaking and can be used for professional and curriculum-based learning to promote robust and equitable learning environments and sustained departmental improvement.

parts.title: The Explore-Before-Explain Guidebook for Science Education: Fostering Active Meaning-Making and Visible Learning
parts.body: This guidebook, "The Explore-Before-Explain Guidebook for Science Education," is designed to help teachers promote active meaning-making in science. It emphasizes an Explore-Before-Explain instructional sequence, which aligns with cognitive science research. This approach means students first build experiences and knowledge using data and evidence before developing explanations. The guidebook also highlights visible learning, where students reflect on their learning and assess their progress, which significantly impacts learning, as supported by John Hattie's 2023 review. The guidebook provides model lessons with specific stopping points for elementary and secondary levels to illustrate grade-span appropriateness and vertical alignment. These sections help teachers understand learning progressions and how lessons can be used across the K-12 spectrum. Preassessments are suggested to gauge student understanding and tailor instruction. The goal is to move beyond simply teaching standards to focusing on purposeful and meaningful instructional design that promotes active meaning-making practices.

parts.title: Explore-Before-Explain: A Powerful Learning Approach
parts.body: This section discusses the Explore-Before-Explain learning approach, which starts with students exploring conceptual science ideas as they occur naturally. This initial exploration is crucial for activating prior knowledge and building interest. Students then generate ideas, test them, and collect evidence to make evidence-based claims. The teacher then provides explanations and elaborations to extend the learning, making them more meaningful by connecting to the students' prior explorations. This approach aligns with Science and Engineering Practices, encouraging students to "do" science rather than just passively learn facts. It emphasizes active meaning-making and firsthand experiences. Once students have developed accurate understandings through exploration, teachers enhance it with timely explanations. This strategy improves comprehension and retention because students actively explore and understand concepts, making them more likely to remember and apply them.

parts.title: Understanding and Applying the Explore-Before-Explain Model
parts.body: This guide helps curriculum designers and teacher leaders understand that effective instructional design is based on how students learn best, evaluating lessons against cognitive science, neuroscience, and developmental psychology research. The goal is to move from traditional teaching, where teachers explain first, to an Explore-Before-Explain (EBE) sequence, especially for those unfamiliar with its supporting research. This module focuses on using an EBE lesson, like "Exploring Sinking and Floating," to connect research to practice and develop a sophisticated view of instructional design. The module uses a model lesson on sinking and floating to illustrate how student curiosity and questions about conceptual science ideas drive active meaning-making. It emphasizes reflection questions (Idea Catcher) throughout, focusing on how student ideas are activated, how the lesson targets relevant concepts, how exploration leads to evidence-based claims, how assessments are incorporated, and what teacher enhancements are needed for deeper understanding. Key materials include a "Watermelon and Grape" probe, a fish tank, water, watermelon, grape, and measuring tools, alongside safety notes for hands-on activities.

parts.title: Module 6: Exploring Fall Time – Applying Active Meaning-Making and Explore-Before-Explain
parts.body: This module, "Exploring Fall Time," focuses on applying active meaning-making and Explore-Before-Explain teaching methods to real classroom scenarios. It aims to refine understanding of how these essential elements appear in different lessons, leveraging cognitive science research that shows actively using information in new situations strengthens understanding. This module is ideal for those who need more examples of how these teaching methods work in practice. The module uses a model lesson involving maple tree seeds to illustrate these concepts. Students observe the seeds, leading to wonderment questions about their shape and function. A graphic organizer called the inquiry planning wheel helps students structure their observations and questions, guiding them to develop scientific experiments. This process helps students understand variables and formulate research questions, such as whether seed size influences fall time. Common student misconceptions about falling objects, like heavier objects falling faster, are also highlighted, emphasizing the importance of eliciting and engaging student ideas.

parts.title: Teaching Science Through Hands-On Activities and Evidence-Based Claims
parts.body: This text focuses on using hands-on activities to teach science, especially by helping students make evidence-based claims. It emphasizes starting with activities teachers already find effective to build a strong foundation for Explore-Before-Explain lessons. The goal is to leverage existing experience and insights to refine teaching methods and ensure alignment with content standards. By analyzing successful activities, teachers can better understand student interaction and connect their findings to scientific principles. The text provides a detailed example using the common experiment of mixing baking soda and vinegar. It outlines how this activity can teach about chemical change and the conservation of matter, aligning with NGSS Lead States standards across different grade levels. It even includes a link to a video, a list of materials, and crucial safety notes, underscoring the practical application of the Explore-Before-Explain model and the importance of engaging students' prior knowledge to create a "need-to-know" situation.

parts.title: Applying Explore-Before-Explain to Practice and Fostering a Growth Mindset
parts.body: This text provides practical guidance on applying the Explore-Before-Explain approach in teaching, focusing on how to activate student thinking and enhance understanding. It emphasizes eliciting students' prior ideas and experiences through thought-provoking questions, discussions, and real-life scenarios, which helps build a personal connection to the material. A crucial step is selecting a conceptual idea, occurrence, or event that resonates with students to anchor learning, making it meaningful and relevant. For example, in a chemistry lesson, teachers might start with familiar chemicals like vinegar and baking soda, asking students to observe and wonder what happens when they mix, or discuss everyday chemical/physical changes like baking a cake. This approach ensures that exploration is engaging and deeply connected to students' lives. The text also includes an "Student Ideas Alert!" section, detailing common misconceptions students have about chemical changes, such as difficulty distinguishing between chemical and physical changes, or believing that matter disappears or that a product was simply “inside” the starting material. Step 3 focuses on Enhancing Understanding by connecting student claims to scientific principles. This involves using enhancement activities to deepen and enrich learning beyond initial explorations, aligning with educational standards. Since hands-on activities alone cannot cover all curriculum, teacher explanations are vital for introducing key terminologies and abstract concepts. These explanations should address essential questions highlighted in the standards, helping students connect their experiences with broader scientific concepts. The text suggests using discussions to illustrate differences between chemical and physical changes, defining key terms like “substance,” and for secondary students, bridging macro-microscopic connections with atoms and molecules. Elaboration activities, such as further explorations and computer simulations (e.g., PhET), are crucial for students to transfer ideas to different situations, fostering a deeper conceptual understanding and application of scientific principles. The text again includes an "Student Ideas Alert!" outlining common student difficulties in understanding chemical combinations at the molecular level and distinguishing chemical from physical changes based on the concept of "substance." Step 4 emphasizes Promoting Reflection on Learning, crucial for students to think critically about their learning process. Teachers act as guides, prompting students with questions like, “How have your ideas changed and why?” Students revisit their initial responses to engagement questions, providing new scientific claims based on data from firsthand experiences. This reflective process helps students connect prior knowledge with new learning, evaluate their understanding, and set future learning goals, fostering a growth mindset. The Explore-Before-Explain framework integrates these four steps (Elicit Ideas, Explore/Claims, Enhance, Reflect) into a coherent instructional sequence, providing a practical template for planning that honors active meaning-making and prior knowledge to make teaching more impactful and responsive to student needs. The chapter concludes by reviewing the "Bannister effect", suggesting that if one person can achieve the "impossible," others can too, applying this growth mindset to educators and students alike. It highlights how teacher beliefs and mindsets are crucial for educational reform and student learning, emphasizing the shift from traditional lecture-based or activity-based teaching to a more student-centered Explore-Before-Explain mindset that prioritizes firsthand experiences and conceptual understanding.
